analysis.one_liner: Repeals federal handgun background checks, waiting periods, and child-safety lock requirements.
analysis.headline: The bill drew zero cosponsors and no committee action; it died in a House subcommittee when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would wipe out several federal gun laws at once: the Brady Act background checks and waiting periods that licensed dealers must run before selling a handgun, the legal tests that restrict firearms based on whether they are 'suitable for sporting purposes,' and the Child Safety Lock Act requirement that dealers supply secure storage or locking devices with handguns. It also repeals the federal distinction between sporting firearms and other firearms in the tax and criminal codes. All of it would take effect immediately on enactment.
analysis.who_benefits: Firearms manufacturers, importers, and licensed dealers would face fewer federal requirements: no background-check contact duty, no safety-device requirement, and an end to the sporting-purposes tests that limited which firearms could be imported or sold. Individual gun buyers would also avoid background checks and waiting periods.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Brady Handgun Violence Prevention Act, ending the federal waiting period and the requirement that dealers contact the national instant background check system before any firearm transfer, and restores the law as it stood before 1993.

Strikes every 'sporting purposes' test from the Internal Revenue Code and federal criminal code, removing the legal line that separated firearms suitable for sporting or recreational use from other firearms.
Repeals the Child Safety Lock Act of 2005, ending the requirement that licensed dealers provide secure gun storage or a safety device with handgun sales, and deletes the related criminal penalties.
Makes all of these changes effective immediately upon enactment.

analysis.who_pays: The general public would bear the safety cost: firearms could change hands without a criminal-record check, and handguns could be sold without locking devices, increasing the risk of guns reaching prohibited buyers and of children finding loaded, unsecured guns.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the Brady Act would eliminate the federal background check that keeps firearms away from people with disqualifying criminal records, and remove the waiting period that applies to handgun purchases.

Repealing the Child Safety Lock Act would end the federal requirement that dealers supply a locking device or secure storage with handguns, which exists to reduce accidental shootings, especially by children.
Eliminating the sporting-purposes distinction would remove the statutory basis used to restrict or block certain firearms, including imports of firearms not suitable for sporting use.

Supporters' strongest point is that background checks and waiting periods burden lawful buyers and add federal paperwork for dealers; an honest supporter would still have to concede that repeal removes a national screening system for every retail gun sale.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are convenience and fewer federal requirements for lawful buyers and dealers. The cost is the removal of a national background-check system, a safety-device mandate, and the sporting-purposes restrictions, all at once and immediately. For anyone not already a gun owner or seller, the bill offers essentially nothing in exchange for the safety rules it strips out, and with zero cosponsors it never came close to being weighed seriously.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees, then to a crime subcommittee, and never got a markup or a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ron Paul introduced the bill in the House on July 21, 2011.
It was referred to both the Judiciary Committee and the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced.
On August 25, 2011, it was referred to the Judiciary Committee's Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security, and no further action ever followed.
Not a single member of the House cosponsored the bill.
It received no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the existing federal background-check system, waiting period, and child-safety lock requirements stayed in force; communities and law enforcement kept rules that gun sellers had hoped to shed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal gun rules stayed in place

for.name: Rep. Ron Paul
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the Brady background-check law, the sporting-purposes restrictions, and the Child Safety Lock Act.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its crime subcommittee and took no further action; the bill never received a markup or floor vote.

sides.party_line_note: No roll-call vote ever occurred; a lone Republican sponsor drew zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan split was ever measured.

industries.note: The bill removes the federal requirements that most directly shape gun commerce: dealer background checks, waiting periods, mandatory safety devices with handgun sales, and the sporting-purposes tests that limit which firearms can be imported. The industry's gain is the public's loss of those safety rules.
